extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalists, policymakers, and general readers interested in news framing and front-page presentation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how different news frames (competitive, explanatory, policy, personality, etc.) are placed on the front page and what placement implies about news value or perceived reader appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-position placement as indicator of importance/news value
rubrics_metrics.description: If one looks at how prominently stories were played on the front page, it tends to slightly reinforce the competitive frames of horse race, conflict, and injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report interprets lead placement as conveying greater news value or urgency. It notes two possible explanations: (a) journalists view conflict/wrongdoing/winning-and-losing as more important or urgent and therefore more deserving of lead placement; or (b) journalists believe competitively framed stories are more likely to appeal to readers and thus should be near the top. Either way, placement is read as a signal of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive frames overrepresented in lead stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive frames (horse race, conflict, and injustice) account for 35% of all lead stories versus their overall representation as 31% of all stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative percent share in the lead position compared to overall share to judge whether a frame is being given prominence. The wording 'slightly reinforce' indicates modest but measurable prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory frames underrepresented in lead position
rubrics_metrics.description: The three explanatory frames (history, process and trends) are placed in the lead position only 8% of the time, even though they represent 13% of all stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory frames are less likely to be given lead prominence and instead appear more frequently lower on the page. This underrepresentation in lead placement can be used as a metric of editorial prioritization against explanatory journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-half placement patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory frames are much more likely to appear on the lower half of the page, where they make up 17%, or nearly one in five stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lower half of the page is described as 'more of a mix' — competitive frames fall to just over a quarter (27%) there, while policy exploration (10% vs. 9% overall) and personality profiles (9% vs. 8% overall) have slight increases versus their general representation. Use lower-half percentages to identify frames that are deprioritized for top placement but still present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare frame share in lead vs overall (relative prominence metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the percentage of a frame among lead stories to its percentage among all stories (e.g., 35% of leads vs. 31% overall for competitive frames; 8% of leads vs. 13% overall for explanatory frames).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparative metric quantifies whether a frame is being privileged or de-emphasized in prominent positions. Positive lead-minus-overall indicates privileging; negative indicates de-emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement interpreted as editorial belief about reader appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Or it could suggest that even if journalists themselves do not think the conflict is that important, they believe that a competitively framed story is more likely to appeal to readers and therefore should be near the top of the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating placement, consider not only newsroom judgments about importance but also perceived audience preferences; placement may reflect commercial/editorial strategies to attract readers rather than intrinsic newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement used to convey urgency or perceived importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the reason, stories framed around competitiveness (conflict, winning and losing and wrongdoing) are placed in such a way as to convey greater news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement (especially lead placement) functions rhetorically: it signals urgency/importance to readers. Evaluations should treat front-page positioning as part of the communicative strategy, not merely layout.
